title: what carries on?
hookLine: if there's no soul packed up and moved, what goes on? one flame lighting the next
last: KARMA · THE THREE JEWELS · SATI · THE FOUR NOBLE TRUTHS · DANA · VESAK

cards: When a grandparent dies, many Buddhist families do more than hold a funeral. Monks chant. Food is offered, and the good of it is dedicated to the one who died.
In many East Asian and Tibetan communities, the prayers go on for forty-nine days, a time, those traditions say, between one life and the next.
Behind it is the question day one left hanging: when a life ends, what happens to everything it set growing? And there's a twist. In the Buddha's teaching, no fixed soul packs up and moves.

teach.h: REBIRTH, NOT A SOUL MOVING HOUSE
teach.b: Many Buddhist traditions teach rebirth: a life, when it ends, is followed by another, shaped by karma, round and round, until someone wakes up.
Teachers often prefer the word rebirth to reincarnation, because nothing solid moves across. An old book of questions gives the best-known picture.
A king asks a monk: is the one who's reborn the same person, or someone else? Neither, says the monk.
Light one lamp from another. Did the flame move over? No.
Is the new flame unrelated? No again: it was lit from the first.

So what passes on is momentum, not a soul. Traditions describe the details very differently: how, where, how soon. Some teachers also point to a version anyone can watch: each moment lit from the last.
If you're not sure about rebirth, you're not behind: plenty of Buddhists practice for years with that question still open.
And for anyone unsure about all of it, there's an old answer too. The Buddha once spoke to villagers who didn't know which teachers to believe.
A kind, clear life is good either way, he told them: if there's another life, it goes well; if there isn't, this one already does.

how: Many Buddhists understand death as followed by rebirth shaped by karma, and mark a death with chanting, merit-making and memorial rites (in many communities over the following seven weeks); traditions describe the process differently, and some teachers also apply it to moment-to-moment experience.

games.q: a king asks a monk: is the one who's reborn the same person, or someone else? what does the monk answer, in the old book of questions?
o: neither: like a lamp lit from a lamp.
games.why: neither the same nor another. the new flame didn't move over, but it was lit from the first.

games.q: build the Pali word: again + becoming.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, notice this breath arriving. On the second, notice that it isn't the one before, and that it came from the one before.
On the third, let it go, and let the next one light itself.

wordCard.voice: Rebirth. Not a soul moving house: one flame lighting the next, carried by karma. Seventh word, and a week's worth.

orig.note: Pali: rebirth, literally 'becoming again'. puna, again; bhava, becoming.

carryVoice: Your line: one flame lights the next. That's week one: seven words, from a meme to a lamp. Tomorrow, the word behind the first truth.
